title: What ADHD is
content: ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) is a developmental condition marked by an ongoing pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity that interferes with functioning. It typically begins in childhood and can continue into adolescence and adulthood, and often occurs alongside other conditions.

title: Inattention vs. hyperactivity/impulsivity
content: Inattention looks like difficulty paying attention, staying on task, or staying organized across settings like home, school, or work. Hyperactivity and impulsivity look like frequent movement or restlessness, talking excessively, interrupting or intruding on others, and trouble waiting one's turn.

title: How ADHD is treated
content: Standard treatment combines medication with psychosocial approaches such as cognitive behavioral therapy, skills and organizational support, and, for children, parent training and school interventions. Mindfulness-based strategies and cognitive training are also being studied.

title: What borderline personality disorder is
content: Borderline personality disorder is a serious condition affecting how a person feels about themselves and others, making everyday functioning hard. It involves difficulty regulating emotions, an unstable sense of self, and instability in relationships.

title: Signs of borderline personality disorder
content: Common experiences include intense mood swings, uncertainty about how one sees oneself, chronic feelings of emptiness, intense anger, and viewing things in extremes (all good or all bad). Self-harming behaviors and recurring thoughts of suicide can also occur and deserve prompt professional support.

title: How borderline personality disorder is treated
content: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) was developed specifically for borderline personality disorder; it uses mindfulness and teaches skills to manage intense emotions, reduce self-destructive behaviors, and improve relationships. Cognitive behavioral therapy can also help by changing inaccurate core beliefs and reducing mood swings, anxiety, and self-harming behaviors.

title: Co-occurring substance use and mental disorders
content: Substance use disorders affect the brain and behavior and can disrupt work, school, and relationships. Many people with a substance use disorder also live with another condition such as depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder at the same time — known as co-occurring disorders.

title: Why they often co-occur
content: Shared factors like stress, trauma, and genetics can contribute to both substance use and other mental disorders. A mental health condition can drive substance use as a way to cope, and substance use can change brain chemistry in ways that raise the risk of other conditions.

title: Treating co-occurring disorders
content: Integrated care that treats mental health and substance use together — in one coordinated place — tends to work best. Options include behavioral therapies such as cognitive behavioral therapy, family-based approaches, and medications that can address more than one condition.

title: What eating disorders are
content: Eating disorders are serious illnesses marked by severe disturbances in eating behaviors, often with intense focus on weight, body shape, or controlling food. They carry a higher risk of medical complications and of co-occurring conditions like depression, anxiety, and substance use.

title: Eating disorders can be treated
content: Eating disorders can be treated successfully, and early detection and treatment support a fuller recovery. Care typically involves psychological therapy, nutritional support, and medical monitoring, sometimes with medication for co-occurring conditions.
